state: Fourteen current registered root records selected after complete reading. Two owners append one scoped note each; old notes, links, aliases, summaries and source scopes are retained.

records.name: Real-world evidence
records.tldr: Evidence about use, benefit or risk derived from analysis of routinely collected health data. Treatment assignment and comparison design determine what it can establish.
records.summary: Real-world data are routinely collected information about health and care; real-world evidence is clinical evidence about a product's use, benefits or risks derived from analysing such data. Records, claims and registries can describe care beyond tightly selected trials. An observational comparison does not assign treatment, so its causal interpretation depends on how groups, outcomes and follow-up are constructed, measured and analysed. More data can improve precision while leaving systematic bias.

links.label: Wikipedia
FDA real-world evidence programme
The Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) statement: guidelines for reporting observational studies.
Specifying a target trial prevents immortal time bias and other self-inflicted injuries in observational analyses
Empirical confidence interval calibration for population-level effect estimation studies in observational healthcare data

notes: An observational study records or reconstructs exposures without assigning them. A cohort follows a defined group over time; a case-control design selects people with and without an outcome and examines earlier exposures; a cross-sectional design measures a population at a time point. Prospective means forward follow-up, not randomized assignment. Such data can describe uncommon harms, care patterns and underrepresented populations. A causal claim about changing treatment requires more than an association. Random assignment reduces treatment-selection bias but cannot guarantee complete follow-up or applicability. In a fictional database, following treated and untreated groups forward from different dates does not randomize them.

When emulating a trial, align eligibility, treatment-strategy assignment and the start of follow-up. Requiring treated people to survive until treatment while starting comparison follow-up earlier can build in a survival advantage. Matching, restriction and statistical adjustment require suitable measurements, assumptions and overlap; poorly measured or unmeasured factors can remain. A large database does not remove systematic error from confounding, selection or measurement. Inspect missing outcomes and follow-up as well as the starting clock.

Two reading rules follow from asking which comparison is being estimated. A consequence of treatment is not automatically a baseline cause of treatment selection, so adjusting for every recorded variable is not a universal remedy and can change the question. Also check the proposed direction of time and causation: developing disease might change an exposure rather than the exposure initiating the disease. These are alternative explanations to examine in a particular study, not findings that either occurred in every observational dataset.

records.name: Cross-trial comparison
records.tldr: Results from separate studies can differ because the people, care or measurements differ. Comparing their headline percentages does not by itself show which treatment works better.
records.summary: A comparison between separate studies must account for differences in participants, treatment, background care, endpoints, clocks and follow-up. Randomisation protects the comparison within a trial; it does not randomise participants between unrelated trials. Formal indirect comparisons can retain within-trial contrasts through a common comparator, but depend on compatible effect modifiers and methods. A higher headline percentage in one study is insufficient to rank treatments.

links.label: The results of direct and indirect treatment comparisons in meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
Cochrane: network comparisons and transitivity
FDA: oncology clinical-trial endpoints (2018)
OncoGuide: cross-trial-comparison (pinned teaching source)

notes: A higher percentage in one paper is a reason to examine its study, rather than proof that its treatment is better. Randomisation protects comparisons within a trial, not between separately conducted trials. Comparing their experimental arms discards that protection. Disease burden, biomarker assay and threshold, prior treatment, background care, dose, endpoint rules, analysis population and follow-up can differ. Formal indirect comparison through a common comparator preserves each trial's treatment-versus-control contrast but still requires compatible questions and methods. Pooling active arms across trials is prone to bias, and even an adjusted indirect estimate remains less secure than a suitable direct comparison (Bucher and colleagues, 1997). Network meta-analysis adds a transitivity assumption: important effect modifiers must be sufficiently comparable across the network. A shared drug name or statistical agreement cannot establish that unmeasured compatibility. Similar endpoint labels can hide different definitions: a clinical benefit rate may include different durations of stable disease. Adjustment for measured differences does not remove every bias, and lower hazard ratios against different comparators cannot automatically rank treatments.

Two fictional single-arm studies each enrol 100 people with the same response definition, assessment period and complete denominator. In the favourable baseline group, A has 40 responses among 80 people (50%) and B has 12 among 20 (60%). In the other group, A has 4/20 (20%) and B 24/80 (30%). Overall, A has 44% response and B 36%, despite B's higher rate in both groups. A enrolled an 80/20 mixture of the two groups, while B enrolled 20/80. Composition reverses the headline ranking. This arithmetic does not establish that B is superior: people were not randomised between studies, and one measured feature cannot resolve every difference.

A fictional vaccine report of 90% recurrence-free at two years in selected postoperative patients cannot be ranked against 30% objective response in a different advanced-disease drug study. Immune response, pathological response, imaging response and survival are different outcomes in different settings. A comparative effect estimate needs a shared clinical question and defensible design. For time-to-event results, align the event definition, origin, assessment schedule, cutoff and follow-up as well as population and care. FDA's December 2018 endpoint guidance warns that external survival comparisons can reflect selection, imaging and supportive-care differences. Neither fictional example certifies an actual indirect comparison.

records.name: Case report
records.tldr: A case report describes what happened to one person or a few, which can reveal a signal or a harm but cannot show what would have happened under a different treatment.
records.summary: A case report documents a clinical course, interventions, outcomes and alternative explanations. It can reveal a signal of benefit or harm without establishing what would have happened under another approach. The CARE reporting guideline includes a timeline, diagnostic assessment, interventions, follow-up, the patient perspective and consent; complete reporting supports appraisal rather than proving treatment causation.

links.label: CARE guidelines: consensus-based clinical case reporting guideline (Deutsches Arzteblatt 2013)
CENT 2015: CONSORT extension for reporting N-of-1 trials (BMJ)

notes: A careful case timeline can preserve an unusual experience and generate questions. Published memorable successes do not supply all treated people as a denominator, so they cannot establish a response probability or treatment ranking. Several scans in one person remain observations from one person. A report usually lacks the concurrent counterfactual outcome under another treatment, and even a rigorous individual comparison would not establish the average effect in everyone sharing a cancer label.

Fictional clinical history: treatment A starts, a procedure is added, treatment B starts and a later scan improves. This establishes improvement during that course, not the separate added contributions of the procedure or B. The earlier treatment, procedure and later treatment can have overlapping lasting influences. Drawing overlapping ribbons represents that possibility and ordering only; it supplies no measured effect size or known duration. Documenting experience and planning an interpretable comparison are different routes to evidence.

A testimonial remains an attributed report until its underlying observations can be checked. In an explicitly fictional blog, a person with metastatic cancer adds an off-label medicine to standard chemotherapy and later scans show shrinkage. Accepting those observations as the example's premise establishes improvement during that combination; it does not isolate the added medicine, its safety or how often the result occurs. Record every intervention and measurement on the timeline and ask for a series or trial with all treated participants, failures, follow-up and a suitable comparison. A company video showing three successes has a different meaning if three of five or three of 500 people were treated. Selected successes do not supply the missing denominator or a personal forecast.

records.name: Meta-analysis
records.tldr: A meta-analysis combines estimates from separate studies with a stated statistical method; it can improve precision, but it cannot repair studies that answer different questions or share the same biases.
records.summary: A meta-analysis statistically combines estimates from studies addressing a sufficiently compatible question. It can be part of a systematic review, which explicitly finds, selects and appraises studies; pooling is not compulsory. The result depends on the studies, their biases, effect definitions, model and weights. A precise pooled mean need not describe every setting or an individual person.

links.label: Higgins, Thompson and Spiegelhalter: a re-evaluation of random-effects meta-analysis (JRSS A 2009)
Cochrane Handbook chapter 10: analysing data and undertaking meta-analyses
PRISMA 2020 statement: reporting systematic reviews (BMJ 2021)
Specifying a target trial prevents immortal time bias and other self-inflicted injuries in observational analyses
Cochrane Handbook chapter 5: identifying and linking multiple reports of one study

notes: A common-effect model targets one underlying effect, while a random-effects model describes a distribution of study effects and its mean. Weights follow the stated estimator, not simply the largest participant count. Clinical and methodological differences, bias and heterogeneity beyond sampling error need investigation; a random-effects calculation does not remove them or make incompatible studies comparable.

A confidence interval for the mean effect differs from a prediction interval for an underlying effect in another comparable study under the model. Neither is a personal prognosis interval. I-squared estimates the proportion of variability in study estimates associated with heterogeneity rather than sampling error; it is neither the percentage of people helped nor the percentage of studies that are wrong. Tau-squared is between-study effect variance on the chosen scale, such as squared score points or squared log risk ratios. These estimates can be uncertain, especially with few studies, and no I-squared cutoff alone makes pooling safe.

Fictional forest example: five studies compare treatment A minus control on the same 0 to 100 symptom scale at day 30. Their effects are -8, -6, -4, -2 and 0 points, each with standard error 2 and weight 20 per cent, so the square areas are equal. The mean is -4.0 points. With a classical moment variance estimate, Q = 10, I-squared = 60 per cent and tau-squared = 6 squared score points. A normal 95 per cent mean interval is about -6.8 to -1.2; the stated 2009 prediction method, using a t distribution with three degrees of freedom, gives about -13.0 to +5.0. The study intervals, mean diamond and wider prediction interval answer different questions. Five studies are few and these intervals are approximate; a negative mean does not imply a negative effect in every setting.

Retain search dates, eligibility, unique study identities, risk of bias, treatment sequence, event definition, starting clock, horizon, effect scale, model, weights, uncertainty and sensitivity analyses. Abstracts, full reports and follow-up of the same participants are linked reports rather than independently weighted trials. Availability related to findings can leave evidence missing. Pooling observational associations does not create randomization or establish one person's treatment benefit. PRISMA promotes transparent reporting; completing its checklist does not certify validity.

Fictional weighted example: two comparable three-year risk differences are -4 and -8 percentage points with supplied weights 0.75 and 0.25. Their weighted mean is -5 points; these stipulated weights are not claimed precision estimates. Correct arithmetic would still not justify pooling if one study starts at randomization and another selects responders at a later landmark. The eligibility, clock and target question must be compared first.

Before pooling, link abstracts, full reports and later follow-up of the same study using registry identifiers, recruiting centres, recruitment dates, treatments, participant counts and baseline characteristics. Different author lists or sample sizes need not mean different trials: a later cutoff or selected analysis cohort can change the reported number. Conversely, one report can describe more than one study. Cochrane Handbook chapter 5 makes the study, rather than the publication, the unit of interest. Retain useful details from secondary reports without counting the same participants again as independent replication.

For the fictional five-study example, Q has four degrees of freedom. The DerSimonian and Laird moment estimate gives tau-squared = 6; each random-effects weight is 1/(4 + 6), normalized to 20 per cent. Each study's normal interval extends 3.92 points either side of its estimate. The pooled standard error is the square root of 2 points. In the specified 2009 method, -4 plus or minus 3.1824463 times the square root of (6 + 2) gives -13.0013 to +5.0013 points, using three degrees of freedom. These choices reproduce this example; they are not a universal recommended estimator.

records.name: Controlled perturbation experiment
records.tldr: Controlled perturbations deliberately change specified factors and compare responses with suitable controls. A model response alone does not prove its mechanism or patient benefit.
records.summary: A controlled perturbation deliberately changes a defined factor and measures the response against appropriate comparison conditions. Vehicle, positive, negative and mechanism controls answer different questions. A reproducible response can support an experimental claim without establishing its proposed mechanism or patient benefit. Baseline growth, timing, dose and the actual unit assigned to treatment matter.

links.label: Hafner et al.: growth rate inhibition metrics correct for confounders in measuring drug sensitivity (Nature Methods 2016)
Measuring cancer drug sensitivity and resistance in cultured cells (Current Protocols in Chemical Biology 2017)
The promise and peril of chemical probes
What exactly is 'N' in cell culture and animal experiments?
Searching for Drug Synergy in Complex Dose-Response Landscapes Using an Interaction Potency Model (2015)
SynergyFinder: a web application for analyzing drug combination dose-response matrix data (2017)
Mutant p53 disrupts mammary tissue architecture via the mevalonate pathway (2012)
Guidelines for the use and interpretation of assays for monitoring autophagy (4th edition)<sup>1</sup> (2021)
Proof-of-concept study linking ex vivo sensitivity testing to neoadjuvant anthracycline-based chemotherapy response in breast cancer patients.

notes: A vehicle control contains the carrier without the active treatment; an untreated condition asks a different question if the carrier has effects. A positive control checks that the assay can detect a known relevant response, while a negative or non-targeting control estimates background under its design. Another independent way to disrupt the same function can support a mechanism, and a rescue restores a function to test whether that reverses the response here. Off-target effects, incomplete restoration and model context limit interpretation. These are questions for matched model, timing and readout; no one control proves specificity or patient benefit, and agreement between similar readouts is not automatically independent mechanistic confirmation.

Keep what changed, the comparator, concentration or dose range, timing, assignment, readout and units, sample identities, replicate structure and variability. Repeated wells address variation under their preparation and allocation; independently obtained biological samples address another source of variation. Many wells from one tumour do not become independent patients, and repetition or a small p-value does not repair a missing comparison. A two-drug experiment needs vehicle, both single drugs and the combination. A larger combination effect than either single drug is not automatically synergy; that claim needs a stated reference model.

Fictional direct counts: vehicle-treated cells increase from 100 to 200 while drug-treated cells remain at 100. The endpoint drug count is half the vehicle count without measured net decline from the starting count, so calling it 50 per cent killing overstates the observation. Slower growth, death and a molecular change require their own readouts; direct death or recovery measurements could address further questions. Hafner and colleagues showed that conventional IC50 and maximal-effect measures depend on cell divisions during an assay and developed growth-rate metrics to address that dependence. A real experimental response does not by itself establish the responsible target or clinical benefit.

A fictional two-drug table normalises remaining viability to vehicle at 100 per cent: A leaves 70, B leaves 80, and combination examples leave 56 or 30. Highest single agent uses the better single-drug effect, a 70 per cent remaining-viability reference here. Bliss independence predicts 0.70 times 0.80 = 0.56, or 56 per cent. Both combinations exceed the HSA effect; 56 matches Bliss while 30 exceeds it at that dose pair. A further combination leaving 65 exceeds HSA but not Bliss. Loewe additivity instead needs equivalent-dose information from suitable individual dose-response curves; this one-point table cannot establish it. Report the model, dose-pair pattern, uncertainty and schedule. Interaction relative to a reference does not identify a biological mechanism, tolerable human exposure or a treatment choice.

A rescue restores a proposed missing function or supply and tests whether a defined effect reverses. Adding a cake mix back after its removal implicates the mixture without identifying flour, sugar or another ingredient; likewise, broad mevalonate add-back does not isolate cholesterol. More specific branch perturbations and appropriate add-backs can narrow the explanation. Partial rescue can reflect incomplete delivery or restoration as well as additional contributors, so it does not prove a second cause. Place the add-back relative to the blocked step: supplying GGPP after an upstream synthesis block is different from inhibiting the transferase that uses GGPP, which the added substrate cannot simply be assumed to bypass. Include restoration-only and matched controls, verify the restored process and distinguish growth, morphology and death. A genetic perturbation also has its own specificity limits.

Attribute each readout to the relevant cells. An ATP-based signal can change through cell number or per-cell metabolism, and slower single-cell mass accumulation does not by itself show death. Direct death measurements and regrowth after washout ask further questions; regrowth concerns surviving cells, not revival of cells already dead. A mixed culture can change composition, and a nonmalignant-cell label alone does not establish a validated healthy-tissue control. Ladan's breast-slice chemotherapy assay was compared with response during preoperative treatment in a defined setting. That assay-specific validation does not validate every postoperative combination, human exposure or clinical decision. An inadequate viable preparation should remain uninterpretable rather than be called resistant.

An unchanged total count can occur while some cells divide and others die. The fictional 100-to-100 treated count establishes no net change. Measuring the fraction that died requires a suitable death readout and denominator.

records.name: Phase 1, 2 and 3 trials
records.tldr: Phase 1 studies dosage and safety; phase 3 compares treatments, often in hundreds or thousands of participants. The protocol determines the design and size, and a phase 3 label is not approval or a promise of benefit.
records.summary: Clinical-trial phases describe development purposes rather than a fixed sample size, assignment method or promise of benefit. Phase 1 studies administration, exposure, safety and dosage, sometimes with early activity measures. Phase 2 asks whether activity and safety support further study in a specified population. Phase 3 compares with a defined alternative and can provide evidence for an approval decision; a phase 3 label is not itself approval. FDA's patient overview illustrates phase 3 with hundreds to thousands of participants, while the actual size follows the protocol's question and information requirements. Phase 4 studies an approved treatment in broader use. Read the protocol because phases can overlap or be combined.

links.label: Wikipedia
FDA: clinical research phases
NCI: how clinical trials work
ICH E9: statistical principles for clinical trials, 1998
Adaptive Randomization of Neratinib in Early Breast Cancer
Adaptive Randomization of Veliparib–Carboplatin Treatment in Breast Cancer
I-SPY 2: an adaptive breast cancer trial design in the setting of neoadjuvant chemotherapy.
ClinicalTrials.gov: overall and site recruitment status fields

notes: A phase 1 activity signal neither establishes benefit nor excludes serious toxicity. A phase 2 study may be single-arm or randomized, and phase 3 may ask superiority or a prespecified non-inferiority question. Sample size follows the question and power or information assumptions; phase number alone does not determine it. A higher phase does not guarantee that a new treatment wins or that one participant benefits. Studying an approved product in phase 4 does not approve every investigated use. A single-arm study has one intervention group; identify its actual external comparison, if any, and endpoint.

I-SPY 2 illustrates an adaptively randomized phase 2 platform. Its 2016 neratinib report describes assignment within biomarker subtypes based on Bayesian probabilities of treatment superiority over control; its veliparib-carboplatin report also describes adaptive assignment within subtype. These are properties of that platform, not every phase 2 trial. Recruitment status is another distinct question: overall recruiting status does not establish an available local cohort slot or that a particular person meets the protocol.

records.name: Randomised trial
records.tldr: A study that assigns eligible participants to interventions by chance. This reduces treatment-selection bias but does not guarantee identical groups, flawless follow-up or benefit.
records.summary: A randomized trial assigns eligible consenting participants to interventions by chance. Concealing the next assignment protects enrolment against foreknowledge; blinding concerns awareness after assignment. These are different design features. Randomization reduces treatment-selection confounding but leaves possible chance imbalance, missing outcomes and limits on applicability. The comparator, endpoint, analysis and conduct determine what the comparison establishes.

links.label: Wikipedia
CONSORT statement: reporting randomised trials
CONSORT 2025 statement: Updated guideline for reporting randomised trials.
ICH E9: statistical principles for clinical trials, 1998
ICH E10: choice of control group

notes: Concealed chance assignment is different from predictable alternation between A and B. Allocation concealment hides the next assignment during enrolment; blinding concerns who knows the assigned treatment afterwards and may not be feasible for every intervention. Report sequence generation, allocation, who was blinded, assigned-group analyses, exclusions, dropout, missing assessments, treatment changes and unequal follow-up. Chance can balance measured and unmeasured factors on average without guaranteeing identical groups in one trial. Random assignment is not random sampling from a population: consenting eligible volunteers remain selected.

Controls can be standard care, standard care plus placebo or another protocol-defined option, not automatically no treatment. A fictional single-group Drug A study showing shrinkage supports an activity question for further study; it does not isolate added survival benefit from selection, natural history and other care. A randomized A-plus-usual-care versus usual-care comparison can test the added effect under sound conduct and analysis, while a volunteer cannot choose their randomized assignment or be promised benefit. A chance-assigned two-group phase 2 trial is randomized even though it is not phase 3.

records.name: Preclinical
records.tldr: Evidence from laboratory, animal and computational work used to study mechanisms, activity and safety. It can guide human studies without establishing patient benefit.
records.summary: Preclinical and nonclinical work studies mechanisms, activity, exposure and safety using specified models. Such experiments can occur before or alongside human studies. Evidence that a model responds does not establish a useful treatment for patients. FDA nonclinical requirements depend on the product and context; its published approaches include justified reductions or replacements of animal studies, so a universal two-species requirement is inaccurate.

links.label: Wikipedia
Studying cancer immunotherapy using patient-derived xenografts (PDXs) in humanized mice
What exactly is 'N' in cell culture and animal experiments?
The ARRIVE guidelines 2.0: Updated guidelines for reporting animal research.
FDA: purpose and safety context of preclinical research
FDA: context-specific nonclinical studies and new approach methodologies
Reporting animal research: Explanation and elaboration for the ARRIVE guidelines 2.0.

notes: In-vitro, in-vivo and human-derived describe experimental setting or origin, not validation of treatment in patients. A cell line can test a direct cell effect, while an immune-intact mouse can test selected tissue and immune interactions; neither reproduces every human cancer, prior treatment or physiology. An immune mechanism needs its relevant components represented and functional. Human tissue grown in a dish or grafted into a mouse remains model evidence about that intervention.

Name the intervention, control, outcome and units before counting replication. The biological unit is the entity about which conclusions are sought, such as a donor. The experimental unit receives an independently assigned intervention; the observational unit is measured. A cage assigned together or a preparation treated before being split can make the animals or wells subsamples. More measured cells do not become more assigned mice. Biological and technical replicate labels vary, so inspect sampling, preparation, allocation and measurement. Repeating runs tests consistency without adding donor identities. Analysing correlated subsamples as independent replicates is pseudoreplication.

Fictional design: each of two donors supplies six wells, three control and three treated. The twelve distinct wells receive independent randomized assignments within donor, separate treatment and no mutual influence, while the analysis retains donor nesting. There are twelve assigned wells and two donor sources, not twelve donors. No cell counts or recommended sample size are supplied. If instead a donor preparation is treated before being split, its wells are subsamples of that assignment. Adding cells does not add wells or donors. This distinction follows from the stipulated allocation, not from a universal rule that wells always are independent.

A controlled fictional mouse study in which local treatment changes a distant tumour can support a distant effect in that model. If a controlled immune-cell depletion reduces that effect, it supports a contribution under those tested conditions. Further steps include safely achievable human exposure, relevant target biology, safety and comparative patient outcomes. Mouse tumour volume is not patient survival, and a laboratory effect size or universal model threshold does not establish clinical benefit. A reproducible mechanism can coexist with an impractical or harmful clinical exposure. These are limits on the inference, not a guarantee that any particular model result will translate.

Retain the model or specimen, treatment and comparator, assigned units and subsamples, exclusions, allocation, blinded assessment, timing, dose, readout units and uncertainty. A cell count, cubic-millimetre tumour volume and named assay signal are different measurements. ARRIVE supports appraisal of animal-study reporting rather than proving a conclusion. Exploratory academic experiments and regulatory safety studies have different purposes and requirements. FDA's context-specific nonclinical approaches, including new approach methodologies, do not validate every model for personal treatment selection.

records.name: N-of-1 trial
records.tldr: A planned comparison within one person, often using repeated treatment periods. Lasting effects and changes over time can make the comparison uninterpretable.
records.summary: An N-of-1 trial studies an individual under a planned comparison. In the multiple-crossover form, treatment periods are assigned within one person and the same outcome is measured repeatedly. Suitability depends on the condition, treatment reversibility, timing and analysis. A sequence of care followed by improvement is not automatically such a trial, and a result for one person does not establish an average effect in a wider population.

links.label: Wikipedia
Wikipedia
Araujo, Julious and Senn: variation and analysis in N-of-1 trials (2016)
Liao and colleagues: N-of-1 carryover and correlated measurements (2021 preprint, version 1)

notes: Specify the question, treatments, period lengths, assigned order, background care, units, observation times and analysis before interpreting results. Inspect whether the actual design uses crossover, random order and blinding. Within-person comparison can reduce between-person differences, but it needs a sufficiently stable condition and interpretable onset and ending of effects. Carryover means an earlier treatment affects a later period; a period effect is change over time apart from the compared treatment, and nearby measurements can be correlated. Random order does not erase these problems. Choose timing and analysis for the actual design and missing observations; there is no universal washout duration.

Fictional symptom example: a planned randomized sequence A, B, B, A uses repeated measurements of the same symptom. The sequence alone proves neither benefit nor adequate transitions between periods. If A persists into B, an apparent A-versus-B contrast may mix current and earlier effects. Progression, lasting immune effects or an irreversible procedure can prevent a meaningful crossover. A cancer-treatment history with surgery and continuing therapy cannot simply be reversed into an untreated comparison. These are interpretation examples, not instructions to change or interrupt care; clinical and research oversight remain separate.

records.name: Trial protocol and statistical analysis plan
records.tldr: The protocol is the rulebook a trial is run by, written before it starts: who can join, what they get, what is measured and when, and how the answer will be calculated; the statistical analysis plan spells out the last part in detail so nobody can choose the analysis after seeing the data.
records.summary:
A protocol is a long document, often more than a hundred pages, that states the rationale and objectives, the design, the eligibility criteria, the treatments and their dose modifications, the schedule of visits and assessments, the endpoints and how each is defined and measured, the sample size and its justification, the interim analyses and stopping rules, the safety reporting rules, and the governance (sponsor, steering committee, data monitoring committee, ethics oversight). The SPIRIT statement lists what a protocol should contain, and journals increasingly publish protocols so that the final report can be checked against them. The statistical analysis plan is a companion document finalised before the data are unblinded that fixes the analysis populations, the handling of missing data and intercurrent events, the order in which endpoints are tested and the alpha each receives, the pre-specified subgroups and the sensitivity analyses. Together they are what makes pre-specified mean something.

Protocols change. Amendments add sites, adjust eligibility when recruitment is slow, revise dose modifications in response to toxicity, or, more consequentially, change the primary endpoint or the sample size; each amendment goes back to the ethics committee and regulators and is dated in the registry record, so a reader can see what changed and when. Deviations are departures from the protocol for individual patients (a missed scan, a dose given outside its window) and are logged and classified by seriousness; a pattern of deviations at one site is a monitoring finding. The strict week-twelve event definition written into BELINDA's protocol, combined with a long manufacturing interval, is a documented example of protocol choices deciding a trial's verdict: the trial found no difference in event-free survival where two similar trials found a large one.

For readers, the protocol answers the questions a paper leaves out: exactly who was eligible, what counted as progression, how many analyses were planned, and whether the headline analysis was the one specified. Registries link to protocols for many trials, and supplementary appendices to trial papers usually contain them. Check the dated plan and access to relevant outcomes to distinguish a confirmatory analysis from planned exploration and later discovery. A small p-value alone does not establish that the analysis was prespecified.

links.label: Wikipedia
SPIRIT statement: standard protocol items for clinical trials
ICH E9 and E9(R1): statistical principles for clinical trials and the estimand framework
ICH E9(R1): estimands, intercurrent events and sensitivity analysis (May 2021)
CONSORT 2025: transparent reporting of randomised trials
NCI: how clinical trials work

notes: Read the protocol and dated analysis plan alongside the report. Write the population, complete assigned strategies, comparator, outcome and assessment, origin and horizon, analysis population and treatment-change rules. Then check precision, bias and applicability separately. Events, sample size, intervals and power concern precision; assignment, assessment, missing outcomes and selected reporting concern bias; eligibility, care sequence, comparator and endpoint concern applicability. A narrow interval cannot fix a systematically biased or mismatched comparison. CONSORT 2025 requests transparent reporting, including plan access, denominators, missing data and harms; a completed checklist is not a certificate of validity.

Two fictional studies answer different questions. Study A treats a single group with metastatic disease after several earlier therapies and observes shrinkage. It describes activity among those treated without supplying a concurrent alternative, comparative survival or quality of life, or postoperative safety. More participants or a phase label cannot erase differences in selection, treatment era or assessment against a historical cohort. Study B randomises people with operable disease to whole treatment sequences and compares first recurrence or death. That can address its assigned strategy under suitable conduct and analysis, while leaving the final unrandomised component unresolved. Resemblance to the participants does not turn an untested action into a tested one.

Keep harms in the same comparison: the number assessed, absolute frequency, severity, onset, duration, symptoms, discontinuation and quality of life. An omitted adverse outcome is not an observed absence of harm, and uncommon or late effects may remain uncertain. More follow-up can clarify one question without supplying a different treatment comparison. Benefits from separate trials with different populations, controls or starting clocks cannot simply be added into a personal estimate.

records.name: Non-inferiority trial
records.tldr: A non-inferiority trial asks whether a new option avoids losing more than an agreed amount of benefit. It can still leave some loss compatible with the data.
records.summary: Non-inferiority seeks to exclude a loss worse than a prespecified, clinically justified margin against an effective control. The endpoint direction, confidence level, population and active-control assumptions matter. A shorter, simpler or less burdensome treatment can motivate the question, but those advantages need evidence of their own. A nonsignificant superiority test does not establish non-inferiority. Adherence, crossover, missing outcomes and analysis-population selection can threaten the conclusion; neither intention-to-treat nor per-protocol is automatically conservative in every design.

links.label: Wikipedia
FDA, 2016: non-inferiority trials, final nonbinding guidance
ICH E9, 1998: analysis sets and statistical planning

notes: Think of replacing a bridge with a lighter design. An agreed limit on lost performance defines what must be ruled out, while the uncertainty around the estimate determines whether it has been ruled out. The analogy does not establish exact equality or safety. Superiority seeks evidence on the favourable side of no difference at the specified inferential level. Non-inferiority rules out the unacceptable worse side; equivalence instead requires excluding unacceptable differences in both directions. A statistically detectable loss smaller than the accepted margin can coexist with non-inferiority.

Less surgery, radiation or systemic treatment can motivate de-escalation, but each strategy needs its own design and acceptable tradeoff. A valid non-inferiority conclusion stays tied to the studied population, comparator, outcome, margin, confidence level and follow-up. It does not mean no participant was harmed, nor that an uncertain result crossing the margin proves harm. Retrospectively declaring non-inferiority after failed superiority lacks the protection of a justified prespecified margin and analysis plan. A planned non-inferiority-then-superiority sequence must address its testing and multiplicity rules.

records.name: Intention-to-treat (ITT) and per-protocol analysis
records.tldr: An intention-to-treat analysis keeps participants in the groups to which they were randomly assigned. Missing outcomes and departures from treatment still need an explicit analysis plan.
records.summary: Intention to treat is an analysis principle preserving the original randomised assignment, including people who change or stop treatment. ICH E9 describes a full analysis set as close as possible to all randomised participants and requires justification of exclusions. Missing outcomes remain a potential source of bias. Per-protocol and modified populations need explicit, prespecified definitions; their roles depend on the clinical question and design. The E9(R1) estimand framework links that question to the treatment conditions, population, outcome, handling of intercurrent events and summary measure. Read the actual report rather than assuming a default analysis population.

notes: The intention-to-treat principle follows everyone in the group to which they were randomly assigned, including people who stop, switch or never start treatment. Keeping that assignment protects the comparison against selection after randomisation; it does not supply an unobserved outcome. ICH E9 describes a full analysis set as close as possible to all randomised participants, with limited, justified exclusions. Its 2021 addendum asks which treatment effect is intended and how treatment changes are reflected. A treatment-policy question uses relevant outcomes despite specified treatment changes, while a hypothetical question targets a stated alternative scenario. Neither label makes missing data harmless.

A per-protocol set uses prespecified requirements such as sufficient treatment exposure, relevant measurements and absence of major protocol violations. It is not simply everyone who finished, and adherence can be related to treatment and outcome. ICH E9 recommends the full analysis set for the primary superiority comparison apart from exceptions. In non-inferiority or equivalence, dilution towards no difference can instead make similarity too easy to claim; the roles of analysis sets and sensitivity analyses need careful justification. Selecting adherent participants does not automatically restore an unbiased causal comparison.

Read the exact definition behind modified intention-to-treat, evaluable and safety populations. A modified set might require a dose, a baseline result or another condition; the name supplies no universal rule. Report all assigned participants, those analysed, exclusion reasons, missing outcomes, grouping and observation window. Safety commonly includes exposed participants, with the actual grouping and exposure denominator specified. These sets can differ from an efficacy comparison. No default analysis population should be assumed for a trial or drug page without checking its report.

Fictional denominator example: four responses among 20 people give 20%. If ten people without documented response are excluded and the four responses remain, four of ten gives 40%. This illustrates how that particular exclusion changes the reported rate; it is not evidence that every evaluable analysis inflates response by a known amount. The reason for missing assessment, prespecified rules and the scientific question still matter.

An analysis population specifies who enters an analysis and how people are grouped. Randomisation protects the comparison in expectation, rather than making observed baseline groups identical. Selecting people afterwards can undo that protection. Think of comparing two school programmes using everyone assigned or just those who completed: completion can depend on the programme and on factors related to the outcome. Per-protocol criteria are prespecified adherence and violation rules, not simply a preference for a tidier result. Those retained are commonly compared in their assigned groups; check the actual protocol. As-treated groups follow actual treatment received, with an explicit rule for non-starters. Safety sets commonly require at least one dose and group by treatment received; definitions remain study-specific.

ICH E9 permits limited, justified exclusions from a full analysis set. For an eligibility violation, its safeguards include measuring the criterion before randomisation, objective detection, equal scrutiny across groups and exclusion of every detected violation of that criterion. Excluding non-starters can preserve the principle only under suitable conditions, such as the decision to start being unaffected by knowledge of assignment. Prespecification alone does not remove treatment-related selection bias. An intention-to-treat label keeps assigned groups; it neither means everyone completed treatment nor supplies missing outcomes.

In a fictional trial with complete follow-up, arm A assigns 100 people: 80 complete treatment and 16 recur; 20 stop and ten recur. All assigned A participants therefore have 26/100 recurrences, or 26%. Arm B also has 26/100. Restrict A to completers and the comparison becomes 16/80 = 20% against 26%, an apparent six-percentage-point advantage created by this selection. No measured frailty difference is specified, and equal observed rates do not prove a zero treatment effect in the population. Removing people changes the question as well as the denominator.

KEYNOTE-522 randomised 1,174 participants with early triple-negative breast cancer, 784 to pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy and 390 to placebo plus chemotherapy. Its 2020 report assessed pathological complete response in the first 602 randomised participants, reporting 64.8% versus 51.2%, a 13.6-percentage-point difference. Event-free survival concerned all 1,174. The early surgical-response subset followed assignment; calling it an as-randomised analysis does not mean that all 1,174 entered that first pCR analysis. In BrighTNess, efficacy was intention-to-treat in 634 participants and safety included 628 who received at least one dose. These efficacy, safety and endpoint-specific denominators answer different questions.

Abraha and Montedori reviewed 475 trials reporting modified intention-to-treat. Eighty per cent excluded participants after randomisation, under varied definitions; their search ended in December 2006. Hollis and Campbell examined reports from four journals in 1997: among 119 mentioning intention-to-treat, 12 excluded non-starters, three did not analyse all participants as allocated, and 89 (75%) had missing primary outcomes. These are distinct, potentially overlapping features, not one combined exclusion count. Check the actual inclusion rules, arm-specific exclusions, reasons and missing-outcome methods rather than trusting the label.

For superiority, retaining assignment commonly protects against overoptimistic selection. For non-inferiority, dilution towards similarity can make a conclusion easier, but nonadherence, crossover and missing data do not invariably bias every study in that direction. A per-protocol comparison may be informative and still selected. An evaluable-response subset can omit people without a scan, changing a response rate; a harms analysis can use a different exposed population. Report the grouping and observation window, and ask which estimand each analysis targets. Neither an intention-to-treat nor per-protocol label guarantees an unbiased answer.

Suppose a fictional report shows an eight-percentage-point advantage among protocol completers, but a two-point, imprecise advantage under intention-to-treat. The latter addresses assignment to the treatment strategy; the former is a selected comparison. Ask who was excluded from each arm, why, when the rules were set and how outcomes after stopping or switching were collected. The larger selected estimate is not automatically the true treatment effect, and the imprecise assigned-group result does not prove no benefit.

records.name: Pre-specified vs post-hoc analysis
records.tldr: An analysis planned before access to the relevant results differs from one developed afterwards. Either can be informative, but its evidence role, timing and search must be clear.
records.summary: Prespecification records an analysis question and method before access to the relevant results. Protocols, statistical analysis plans and dated amendments distinguish confirmatory questions from planned exploration and later discoveries. A prespecified analysis can still be exploratory or imprecise. A post-hoc analysis can generate useful hypotheses, but choosing a favourable result and then calling it prespecified or independently validated does not provide confirmation.

notes: Keep the dated protocol and analysis plan, endpoint and starting clock, population, methods, marker rule, evidence role and multiplicity strategy. Record amendments, their reasons and access to unblinded results. An amendment made without relevant outcome access differs from choosing an analysis after seeing a favourable result. Planning cannot supply missing events or precision, and a prespecified exploratory question remains exploratory. A plan uploaded after results calls for earlier versions and access dates; that timing alone establishes neither misconduct nor confirmation.

Fictional analysis example: event-free survival is the primary endpoint, a marker subgroup is planned as exploratory, and after opening the results investigators search 12 additional cutoffs and select the smallest p-value. Keep all three evidence roles and the entire 12-cutoff search. The schematic choices contain no supplied p-values or measured threshold coordinates. Locking the discovered cutoff permits an appropriate independent test; it neither changes the original analysis role nor confirms treatment-selection utility by itself.

A p-value describes compatibility of the data with a specified statistical model under its assumptions. It is not the probability that the subgroup claim is true. Selection among many analyses changes how an attractive p-value should be interpreted.

records.name: Subgroup analysis (forest plots)
records.tldr: A subgroup analysis compares effects in defined groups. A striking estimate or different significance labels do not by themselves establish that treatment effects differ.
records.summary: Subgroup analyses examine whether treatment effects differ across defined groups. Report the effect scale, interaction analysis, uncertainty, multiplicity and whether the groups and methods were specified before relevant results were available. Wide intervals, selected cutoffs and missing specimens can limit interpretation. A significant result in one group and a nonsignificant result in another is not itself a test of their difference. Confirmation and treatment-selection utility require additional evidence.

notes: A small subgroup chosen because of its observed result can motivate a new study without establishing who benefits from treatment. Compare treatment-effect estimates directly using an appropriate interaction analysis, uncertainty and multiplicity control; different significance labels in two groups are not evidence that the effects differ. A group defined by response after treatment is also different from a baseline category because treatment can affect who enters it.
